260.title: For heaven's sake (Avot 2:12)
260.hook: let your friend's property be as dear as your own, and do everything for heaven's sake
260.howItsDone: The phrase leshem shamayim is used for acts done with a higher purpose, and some Jews say a short declaration of intention before performing a commandment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ayin tovah: Rabbi Joshua warned against the begrudging eye. Your line was glad when others do well.

Oh, for heaven's sake. It comes out when the printer jams, when the dog gets into the trash, when someone takes the last parking spot. It's what people say when they're fed up. Hebrew has a phrase with almost the same words. Leshem shamayim, for the sake of heaven, isn't a sigh of frustration at all. It's a way of living. And it comes from Rabbi Yose, the student his teacher called the pious one.
screen: `OH, FOR HEAVEN'S SAKE.` → `A SIGH, OR A WAY OF LIVING?` → `RABBI YOSE, THE PIOUS ONE.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Yose says three things. First: let your friend's property be as dear to you as your own. Treat the borrowed ladder like it's yours. Better, actually, because it isn't. Return it on time, clean, working. Second: prepare yourself to learn Torah, because it isn't an inheritance. You can inherit a house from your parents, but not their learning. Even the child of the greatest scholar starts from the first page and does the work himself. Third: let all your deeds be for the sake of heaven. Heaven, here, is a respectful way of saying God. Whatever you do, let it point toward something higher than yourself. Not only praying and studying. Everything. Later Jewish teachers took this very far. Maimonides wrote that even eating and sleeping can be for the sake of heaven, if you do them to keep your body healthy so you can do good. The meal is still a meal. The nap is still a nap. What changes is the reason. Put the three together. Other people's things matter as much as yours. What's worth having has to be earned, not handed down. And ordinary life can be aimed at something holy, printer jams and parking lots included. Even the moment you want to say oh, for heaven's sake can remind you what the Hebrew phrase means.

segments.voice: Think of something completely ordinary you'll do today: making lunch, commuting, answering email, returning something you borrowed. Ask what higher purpose it could serve: feeding someone well, getting somewhere to help, keeping a promise. You don't have to change the act; just let the reason point a little higher.
Leshem shamayim. For the sake of heaven: Rabbi Yose's teaching that all your deeds, even the ordinary ones, can be done for the sake of heaven.
Your line: return it in good shape. A borrowed ladder can point toward heaven too. Day two hundred sixty, done.

261.title: Not a routine (Avot 2:13)
261.hook: don't make your prayer a fixed routine but a plea for mercy
261.howItsDone: Jewish prayer follows fixed texts in the siddur, said three times a day, and the tradition asks for kavanah, inner intention, and makes room for personal requests in one's own words within the Amidah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, leshem shamayim: Rabbi Yose said let all your deeds be for the sake of heaven. Your line was return it in good shape.

Love you, bye. You've said it at the end of a call so fast it came out as one word. Loveyoubye. You meant it, sort of, but your mind was already on the next thing. Anything said every day can wear smooth like that, like a stone in a river. Traditional Jewish prayer is said three times a day, mostly from a fixed prayer book. So the rabbis faced a real problem: how do you say the same words thousands of times without them turning into loveyoubye? Rabbi Shimon, the fourth of the five students, has an answer.
screen: `LOVEYOUBYE.` → `A STONE WORN SMOOTH.` → `THE SAME WORDS, THREE TIMES A DAY.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Shimon says: be careful with the Shema and with prayer. When you pray, don't make your prayer keva, fixed, but a plea for mercy before God. Then he gives a verse from the prophet Joel: God is gracious and full of compassion, slow to anger. The same verse begins, in the JPS translation, "rend your heart, and not your garments." Tear open your heart, not just your clothes. The outward sign isn't enough. The Talmud stops to ask what keva actually means, and gives several answers. One sage says: prayer that feels like a burden, a chore to get through. Others say: prayer that isn't said as a real request, the way a person actually pleads. Another says: prayer where you can't add anything new. One rabbi admitted he could add something new, but was afraid he'd lose his place in the prayers. A very human moment. Here's the interesting part: nobody says throw out the prayer book. The fixed words stay. They let a whole community pray together, with shared words, at shared times. Rabbi Shimon asks only that the fixed words not make you fixed. The Hebrew word for that inner attention is kavanah: intention, direction, aiming the heart. The words are the same. You're the one who arrives new. He ends with one more line: don't be wicked in your own eyes. Don't give up on yourself. Some commentators explain that someone who writes himself off stops trying to turn back.

segments.voice: Pick words you say every day on autopilot, a blessing, a greeting, a goodnight, love you, bye, and say them silently, very slowly, meaning every word, as if for the first time. If you pray, add one sentence of your own words to a prayer you already know; if you don't, just let one honest sentence of what you need rise up.
Keva. Fixed, routine: the word in Rabbi Shimon's warning not to let prayer become it, but a real plea from the heart, with kavanah.
Your line: not rote. The same words, with a new heart each time. See you tomorrow.

262.title: Know who you work for (Avot 2:14)
262.hook: be eager to learn, and know before whom you labor
262.howItsDone: Jewish learning makes room for hard questions, and the words 'know before whom you stand' appear above the ark in some synagogues as a reminder during prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, keva: Rabbi Shimon asked that prayer never become routine, but stay a real plea. Your line was not rote.

A kid at the dinner table, usually when a guest is there, asks the big one. How do you know God is real? Or, why do we even do this? The adults glance at each other, and somebody says, eat your peas. Today's sage, the last of the five students, is Rabbi Elazar, usually identified as Elazar ben Arach: the student whose answer won, the one with the good heart. His saying starts by telling you to be ready for that question.
screen: `THE QUESTION AT THE DINNER TABLE.` → `EAT YOUR PEAS.` → `ELAZAR BEN ARACH.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Elazar says: be eager to learn Torah. Know what to answer an apikoros. And know before whom you toil, and that your employer can be trusted to pay you the wage of your work. The strange word first. Apikoros echoes the name Epicurus, a Greek philosopher who taught that the gods take no interest in human affairs. In rabbinic Hebrew, an apikoros is a scoffer, someone who mocks the faith and its teachers. Rabbi Elazar doesn't say avoid them, or shout them down. He says study well enough to answer. Don't be caught with only eat your peas. There's a quieter reading too: sometimes the skeptic is the voice in your own head at two in the morning, and knowing what to answer means learning enough to face your own questions honestly. Then the second half: know before whom you toil. All your learning and work happen in front of someone. A related line in the Talmud, sometimes written above the ark in synagogues, says know before whom you stand. Then a picture from the workplace: your employer is trustworthy, and will pay your wages. The employer, in this saying, is God. In the saying's picture, the work put into learning and living well isn't lost, even when no one else seems to notice. Learn hard, be ready for hard questions, and remember who you're really working for.

segments.voice: Let one hard question come up, about faith, or meaning, or why people do what they do, your own or one a child or friend has asked you. Don't rush to answer it; just hold it honestly. Then ask what one thing you could learn, a book, a person to ask, a page of text, that would help you answer it better.
Apikoros. A scoffer, a skeptic of the faith: the one Rabbi Elazar says to study hard enough to answer, while remembering before whom you toil.
Your line: know before whom you toil. A hard question deserves a real answer. That's day two hundred sixty-two.

263.title: The day is short (Avot 2:15)
263.hook: Rabbi Tarfon: the day is short, the work is great, the workers are lazy
263.carry: start with the thing that matters most
263.howItsDone: Rabbi Tarfon's saying is often quoted in Jewish teaching as a reminder that life is brief and there is much good to do, and it is usually paired with the saying that follows it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, apikoros: Rabbi Elazar said know what to answer the skeptic, and know before whom you toil. That was your line.

It's four in the afternoon. You look at your list. Somehow the easy things got done: the emails, the small errands, a very thorough reorganization of your desk. And the one hard thing, the thing that actually mattered, is still at the top of the list, untouched. The light is already changing. Rabbi Tarfon, a priest who lived through the years when the Temple was destroyed, knew that four o'clock feeling. He put it into five short phrases that sound like a foreman shouting across a building site.
screen: `FOUR IN THE AFTERNOON.` → `THE HARD THING, UNTOUCHED.` → `A FOREMAN ON A BUILDING SITE.`

segments.voice: The day is short. The work is great. The workers are lazy. The reward is great. And the master of the house is pressing. Start with his world. In ancient Israel, a day laborer worked from sunrise to sundown, and the Torah said he had to be paid before the sun went down. So the whole day had a clock on it. When the light's gone, it's gone. Now read the saying as a picture of a life. The day is short: a lifetime goes faster than anyone expects. The work is great: so much to learn, so much good to do, so many people who need something. The workers are lazy: that's people, honestly. Not wicked. Just distracted, tired, reorganizing the desk. The reward is great: the work is worth it, more than anyone can see. And the master of the house is pressing: God, in this picture, is the owner of the field, and there's a gentle urgency in the air. Notice what Rabbi Tarfon doesn't say. Not you're a failure. Not it's hopeless. He names the situation as plainly as a foreman would, and trusts you to do the math. If the day is short and the work is great, you start with the thing that matters most. And if that sounds like a lot of pressure, hold on. Tomorrow, the very next line of Pirkei Avot, from the same Rabbi Tarfon, lets you breathe again.
screen: `FIVE SHORT PHRASES.` · `PAID BEFORE SUNDOWN.` · `A LIFE IS A WORKING DAY.` · `START WITH WHAT MATTERS MOST.` · then, large: `THE DAY IS SHORT.`

segments.voice: Let today's list come to mind, and notice the item you keep circling: the hard one, the one that matters. Don't feel guilty about it; just see it clearly. Then picture the first five minutes of doing it: where you'll sit, what you'll open, the first sentence, the first call, the first step.
Rabbi Tarfon, the priest who named the day short, the work great, the workers lazy, the reward great, and the master of the house pressing.
Your line: start with the thing that matters most. The light doesn't wait. Two hundred sixty-three days in.

264.title: Not yours to finish (Avot 2:16)
264.hook: Rabbi Tarfon: it is not yours to finish the work, nor are you free to give it up
264.howItsDone: Rabbi Tarfon's words are among the most quoted in Pirkei Avot, often cited by Jews working on long efforts for justice, learning and repair that no one person can complete.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Tarfon the foreman: the day is short, the work is great. Your line was start with the thing that matters most. Today, he lets you breathe.
screen: `START WITH THE THING THAT MATTERS MOST.`

segments.voice: Some problems are too big for one life. Hunger. Loneliness. A broken family pattern that goes back generations. A neighborhood that needs a hundred things. You look at them and two feelings arrive together. One says, it's hopeless, why bother. The other says, it's all on me, and I'm failing. Both are exhausting, and both make people quit. In the very next line, Rabbi Tarfon answers both at once, in a sentence people have been writing on walls and in notebooks ever since.
screen: `TOO BIG FOR ONE LIFE.` → `HOPELESS, OR ALL ON ME.` → `THE VERY NEXT LINE.`

segments.voice: It is not upon you to finish the work. But you are not free to walk away from it. Two halves, and each answers a different fear. To the one who says it's all on me: it isn't. You were never asked to finish. The work is bigger than one life, and it was always meant to be. You do your part, and hand it on. To the one who says it's hopeless: you're still not free to quit. The Hebrew phrase is ben chorin, a free person, the same words used for a slave who's been set free. You're not that kind of free, not from this. You still owe your piece. The Talmud has a story that fits right beside it. Honi, a famous sage, is walking along a road when he sees an old man planting a carob tree. How long until it gives fruit? Honi asks. Seventy years, says the man. Do you really think you'll live seventy more years? And the old man answers: I found carob trees in the world when I came into it. My ancestors planted them for me, and I'm planting for my children. He won't finish. He won't eat the fruit. And he plants anyway. Rabbi Tarfon ends by returning to the employer from two days ago: the one you work for is trustworthy, and will pay your wage. You don't have to see the harvest to know the planting counts.
screen: `NOT UPON YOU TO FINISH.` · `NOT FREE TO WALK AWAY.` · `BEN CHORIN: A FREE PERSON.` · `HONI AND THE CAROB TREE.` · then, large: `DON'T FINISH, DON'T QUIT.`

segments.voice: Think of one big problem that weighs on you, in your family, your town, the world, and let yourself feel how big it is. Then set down the part that was never yours, finishing it, and feel that weight go. Now find your piece, the small, real part you could do, one call, one hour, one kindness, one seed, and hold it in your hands.

Your line: don't finish, don't quit. The old man planted anyway. Day two hundred sixty-four is planted.

265.title: Who is wise? (Avot 4:1)
265.hook: Ben Zoma: the wise learn from everyone; the rich are content with their lot
265.howItsDone: Ben Zoma's four questions are often taught in Jewish classes, and 'who is rich? one who is happy with his portion' is a saying people quote about contentment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ben chorin: the work isn't yours to finish, and you're not free to quit. Your line was don't finish, don't quit. Today, a skip ahead to chapter four.

The Talmud tells a story about a sage named Ben Zoma. One day he stood on a high step on the Temple Mount and looked down at the enormous crowds of pilgrims. Instead of being annoyed by all the people, he said a blessing. Think how hard the first human had to work for a piece of bread, he said. Plowing, sowing, reaping, threshing, grinding, kneading, baking. And I wake up, and all of it's been done for me, by all these people. That's the man who opens chapter four of Pirkei Avot, with four questions.
screen: `BEN ZOMA ON THE TEMPLE MOUNT.` → `ALL THESE PEOPLE.` → `FOUR QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Who is wise? Who is strong? Who is rich? Who is honored? Each answer flips what you'd expect. Today, two of them. Who is wise? Not the one with the most degrees. The one who learns from every person. Then a verse from the Psalms that, in its plain sense, sounds almost boastful. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "I have more understanding than all my teachers." But the Mishnah reads the Hebrew another way, which the words can bear: from all my teachers I gained understanding. Every person is a teacher. The toddler who asks why. The coworker you find difficult. The stranger who does a job you've never noticed. Everyone knows something you don't. Who is rich? Not the one with the most. The one who's happy with his portion, what he already has. Another psalm backs it up: when you eat the work of your own hands, you'll be happy, and it will be well with you. Now back to the Temple Mount. Ben Zoma looked at a huge crowd and saw bakers, farmers, weavers, all the people whose work fed and clothed him. He learned from everyone, and he was grateful for what he had. Wise and rich at once. Both begin in the same place: paying attention to the people around you, and to what you've already been given. Tomorrow, the other two questions.
screen: `FOUR QUESTIONS THAT FLIP.` · `WISE: LEARNS FROM EVERY PERSON.` · `A PSALM, READ ANOTHER WAY.` · `RICH: HAPPY WITH HIS PORTION.` · then, large: `LEARN FROM EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Think of three people you'll likely see today, including one you don't especially like, and for each one ask: what does this person know that I don't? A skill, a kind of patience, a way of seeing; there's always something. Then, for a breath or two, notice something you already have that's enough.
Ben Zoma, the sage who asked who is wise. His answer: the one who learns from every person. And who is rich? The one who's happy with what he has.
Your line: learn from everyone. The crowd is full of teachers. That's two hundred sixty-five.

266.title: Who is strong? (Avot 4:1)
266.hook: Ben Zoma: the strong master their impulses; the honored honor others
266.howItsDone: Jewish ethics describes the lifelong work of mastering the yetzer hara, the selfish inclination, and Ben Zoma's answer is a common text for that work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ben Zoma: the wise learn from every person, and the rich are happy with their portion. Your line was learn from everyone.

Somebody cuts you off in traffic. Your hands tighten on the wheel. The horn is right there. So is a gesture, and a whole paragraph of words you'd never say in front of your grandmother. And then, sometimes, something else happens. You breathe out, let it go, and the car ahead just becomes a car again. Nobody sees it. Nobody gives you a medal. But Ben Zoma has a name for what just happened. He calls it strength.
screen: `CUT OFF IN TRAFFIC.` → `THE HORN IS RIGHT THERE.` → `YOU LET IT GO.`

segments.voice: Ben Zoma's third question: who is strong? The Hebrew word is gibor, the word for a warrior, a hero. His answer: the one who conquers his own inclination. The urge, the impulse, the thing that wants to explode or grab or get even. Then a verse from Proverbs, which in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation reads: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city." Conquering a city is a king's glory. Ruling your own temper is greater. The battlefield Ben Zoma cares about is inside you. Then the fourth question: who is honored? You'd think the one everyone bows to. Ben Zoma says: the one who honors others. The verse he brings is about God: those who honor Me, I will honor. Some commentators notice that Ben Zoma applies it to people, and explain that honoring people made in God's image is a way of honoring God. There's a practical truth in it too. Honor you demand is fragile. Honor you give away tends to come back. So the four questions flip the world: the wise learn, the strong hold back, the rich are content, and the honored give honor. And that ends a week of sayings: return it in good shape, not rote, know before whom you toil, start with the thing that matters most, don't finish, don't quit, learn from everyone, and today, strong is self-mastered.
screen: `GIBOR: THE WARRIOR.` · `THE ONE WHO CONQUERS HIS URGE.` · `SLOW TO ANGER, BETTER THAN MIGHTY.` · `HONORED: THE ONE WHO HONORS.` · then, large: `STRONG IS SELF-MASTERED.`

segments.voice: Think of a situation where your temper usually wins: a certain person, a certain tone of voice, a certain kind of mess in the kitchen. Picture it starting and feel the heat rise; then, in your imagination, pause for one slow breath out and let the heat pass through you without doing anything. That pause is the strength, so rehearse it a few times.
Gibor. The Hebrew word for a warrior, a hero. Ben Zoma's answer to who is strong: the one who conquers his own inclination. And who is honored? The one who honors others.
Your line: strong is self-mastered. Ruling your spirit beats taking a city. Day two hundred sixty-six, done.
